summary: Rand's comments on the socket conventions of RFC 167. It agrees with the conclusion that a major NCP overhaul is needed, but disagrees about the socket length. Because of limited storage in the TIP, Rand will assign sockets with the high-order 16 bits zero.

plainLanguage.summary: Rand supports revising socket conventions but explains that its Terminal IMP has limited storage. The RFC describes a socket-number arrangement that fits that constraint.

subtitle: Rand comments on socket naming and its storage limits.

tldr.problem: Rand agreed that socket conventions needed attention but faced a storage constraint in its Terminal IMP.
tldr.mechanism: Rand's assigned sockets would have their high-order 16 bits set to zero, and the RFC diagrams its socket-name fields.
tldr.outcome: Rand says repeatable socket names are needed for initial contact sockets, but not for ordinary user and server processes.

sections.title: Comments on Socket Conventions
sections.content: Rand's authors agree with the conclusions in RFC 167, especially the need for a major NCP overhaul. Their main difference concerns socket length. Because of a storage concern in the Terminal IMP, Rand planned to assign sockets with the high-order 16 bits set to zero.
sections.plainLanguage: Rand agreed that the network control software needed a major update. It could not use the proposed socket length in the same way because of storage limits.

sections.title: Socket Names and Repeatability
sections.content:
The RFC says repeatable socket names are not necessary for Rand's current and planned user processes, or for server processes except for initial contact sockets. It presents a diagram of the socket-name fields, including an administratively assigned portion and fields used for initial contact or dynamic assignment.

The authors note that their scheme corresponds to conventions at UCSB and UCLA/CCN.
sections.plainLanguage: Most processes do not need to reuse the same socket name every time. Initial contact sockets are the exception, and Rand says its scheme matches two other sites.

sections.title: Implementation Constraint
sections.content: The report ties the zero high-order bits directly to the Terminal IMP storage issue. It comments on the earlier socket convention discussion rather than defining a complete network-wide replacement convention.
sections.plainLanguage: This note explains Rand's implementation choice and its reason. It does not set a new convention for every host.
